**Observation Log:**

- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/05/29 (Mon) 02:55
- [USER] User inquired about traditional tattoo designs and techniques used by Maori tribes in New Zealand.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The Maori people of New Zealand have a rich tradition of tattooing known as ta moko.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Traditional tattoo designs and techniques used by Maori tribes include:
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Spiral shapes: Represent life, growth, and eternity.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Koru: Rounded shapes representing new life, growth, and the unfolding of a fern frond.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Tiki: A carving or tattoo of a human figure with prominent eyes, representing the spiritual connection between humans and the divine.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Whakairo: Intricate, swirling designs used to decorate weapons or carvings, also found in ta moko designs.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Tapu: A series of lines representing the restrictions of the spiritual world.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Kowhaiwhai: Decorative patterns often found on the rafters of meeting houses, representing familial connections and relationships.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Chiseling: Some traditional Maori tattoo artists use a chisel to cut designs into the skin instead of a needle.
  - [ASSISTANT_SAID] Ink rubbing: A technique involving rubbing ink into cuts made on the skin, leaving a permanent tattoo.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Ta moko remains an important cultural tradition for the Maori people, with many choosing to get traditional designs to honor their cultural heritage.
- [USER] User expressed fascination with Maori culture and requested more information about the history of ta moko and its evolution over time.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Ta moko has a long history in Maori culture, dating back to ancient times.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The earliest forms of ta moko were done using uhi, a type of chisel made from sharpened shark teeth.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The uhi was dipped in ink made from a mixture of ash and oil, and tapped with a mallet to create the tattoo design.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The process was extremely painful and took several days to complete, reserved for important figures in Maori society.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] In the 19th century, European tattooing methods led to a decline in the practice of ta moko.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Many Maori began opting for cheaper, faster, and less painful tattooing methods, leading to a near loss of traditional Maori tattooing.
